title: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
summary: Describes an updated version of the Encapsulating Security Payload, which provides a mix of security services in IPv4 and IPv6. These include confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, anti-replay protection, and limited traffic flow confidentiality. It replaces RFC 2406 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protects IP traffic between hosts or security gateways. Depending on the negotiated settings, it can encrypt data, verify its integrity and reject replayed packets.

subtitle: ESP protects IP traffic with encryption, integrity checks and replay detection.

tldr.problem: IP traffic may be exposed to reading, modification or replay while it travels between security peers.
tldr.mechanism: ESP adds a security identifier and sequence number, protects a payload and trailer with negotiated algorithms, and can attach an integrity check value.
tldr.outcome: ESP defines transport and tunnel modes, replay protection and optional traffic-flow padding. RFC 4303 obsoletes RFC 2406.

today: RFC 4303 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2406. The batch metadata lists no later RFC as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Security Services ESP Provides
sections.content:
ESP is a protocol for applying security services to IPv4 and IPv6 traffic. Depending on the Security Association (SA), it can provide confidentiality, integrity, data-origin authentication, replay protection and limited traffic-flow confidentiality.

Confidentiality and integrity are separate choices, but at least one must be selected. The RFC requires implementations to support integrity-only and combined confidentiality-and-integrity service. Replay protection can be enabled only when integrity is enabled, because the sequence number must be protected.
sections.plainLanguage: ESP can hide packet contents, detect changes and reject repeated packets. The selected services depend on the security settings shared by the communicating peers.

sections.title: The ESP Packet Fields
sections.content:
An IP header identifies ESP with protocol number 50. The ESP header begins with a Security Parameters Index (SPI), which helps the receiver find the right SA, and a sequence number that increases for each packet.

The payload is followed by padding, a pad-length field and a Next Header field that identifies the protected data. An Integrity Check Value (ICV) may follow. When a separate integrity algorithm is used, it covers the ESP header, payload and trailer. Padding can meet encryption alignment needs; separate traffic-flow padding can add bytes to obscure packet lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: The ESP header identifies the security settings and numbers each packet. The protected payload and trailer say what data is inside, while an optional integrity value helps detect changes.

sections.title: Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
In transport mode, ESP follows the IP header and protects the next-layer protocol information. The original IP header remains outside the protected payload.

In tunnel mode, the entire original IP packet, including its header, is protected as the payload. A new outer IP header carries addresses for the IPsec peers. The RFC allows the inner and outer headers to use different IP versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport mode protects the data after the original IP header. Tunnel mode protects the whole original packet and adds a new outer IP header.

sections.title: Negotiated Encryption and Integrity Algorithms
sections.content:
The SA specifies the encryption and integrity algorithms used for ESP packets. The protocol allows separate algorithms or a combined algorithm that performs encryption and integrity checking together. Each packet includes or derives any synchronization information needed to process packets that arrive out of order or after loss.

The RFC leaves the mandatory algorithm list to a separate document so algorithm requirements can change independently. Encryption and integrity may each use a NULL algorithm in the circumstances described by the RFC, but both must not be NULL at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: The SA tells both endpoints which encryption and integrity methods to use. ESP supports separate methods and methods that perform both jobs together.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Rejecting Replays
sections.content:
For separate algorithms, the sender forms the payload and trailer, adds needed padding, encrypts, then computes the ICV. On receipt, the receiver locates the SA using the SPI and checks the sequence number and integrity before passing decrypted data onward. If no valid SA exists or integrity verification fails, it discards the packet.

Replay protection uses a sliding receive window to detect duplicate or too-old sequence numbers. A 32-packet window is the minimum required for 32-bit sequence numbers; 64 is preferred as the default. Extended Sequence Numbers provide a 64-bit counter while sending only the low-order 32 bits in the packet.

IP fragments must be reassembled before ESP processing. A packet that still appears fragmented when offered to ESP must be discarded. Next Header value 59 marks a dummy packet, which the receiver discards without error.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver finds the matching security settings, checks that the packet is authentic and not a replay, then decrypts it. Packets with failed checks, no matching SA or the dummy-packet marker are discarded.

sections.title: Auditing and Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
If a system supports auditing, its ESP implementation must let an administrator enable or disable ESP auditing. The RFC names events including a missing SA, an apparent fragment, sequence-number overflow, a failed anti-replay check and a failed integrity check. It does not require a receiver to send a response to the apparent sender.

A conforming implementation must support the ESP processing described for unicast traffic and the additional requirements in the IPsec architecture. An implementation that supports multicast must also meet the multicast requirements. The separate algorithm requirements are maintained outside this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations can record specified packet failures for administrators. The RFC also requires support for its ESP packet processing rules and refers to a separate document for required algorithms.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 2406
sections.content:
RFC 4303 replaces RFC 2406. The update adds Extended Sequence Numbers, combined encryption-and-integrity algorithms, additional traffic-flow padding and dummy packets marked with Next Header 59. It also moves mandatory algorithm requirements to a separate RFC.

ESP has no version field or built-in version negotiation. When none of the new features is used, the RFC says the packet format is identical to the earlier version. The security considerations point readers to the IPsec Security Architecture for additional guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition adds optional ways to handle packet numbering, combined algorithms and traffic-flow padding. ESP itself does not identify its version, so peers need compatible settings.
